text:
Not just any quango, Natural England is the only public body that exists to legally protect the jewels in the crown of English nature – places increasingly under threat in a country that is overseeing an ongoing and devastating decline in its natural world.
Ecologists who work for Natural England are independent, and have the legal duty to scrutinise political decisions and ensure that short-term gallops for growth are not allowed to bulldoze forever rare and declining habitats.
They are tasked with the protection of many varied sites from the dense woodland of Lodge Hill in Kent, where the last nightingales can still be heard, to the grasslands of Thetford in Norfolk, home to declining species such as the long-eared owl and lesser spotted woodpecker.
It is Natural England that is creating 2,700 miles of coast path that will be the King Charles lll national coast path – the first continuous trail around England and the longest managed coastal walking route in the world.
Natural England’s scientists oversee and regulate 5,000 environmental gems, including sites of special scientific interest, special areas of conservation and wetlands protected under the internationally binding Ramsar convention.
They work with farmers across the country on the long-term restoration of habitats, under landscape recovery schemes that can last more than 20 years, helping them restore peatlands, rewild rivers, reduce flooding and reduce wildfire risks.
Ministers argued on Monday that Natural England was a block to development. But there is almost no evidence that nature, and regulations that protect it, are an obstruction to development, according to the government’s own analysis.
From the other side, environmentalists criticise Natural England for being too weak, pointing out that it has fallen behind on creating new protected sites to ensure the enhancement and protection of nature after deep cuts to its budget.
But the answer, most environmentalists agree, is to restore its effectiveness, not to abolish it.
It is not clear what would replace Natural England. It could be that it is subsumed within the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, with ministers ultimately in charge.
“In that scenario you immediately lose the independence and you lose the statutory duty to protect nature,” said Alexa Culva, an environmental lawyer from RSK Wilding.
“Defra is a government department, which we have already seen is under political pressure to make short-term decisions to enhance growth, that are often in conflict with protecting nature.”
Similarly, a Burnham approach, of moving the duties of Natural England to local mayoral authorities, would mean no independence and no legal duty to protect nature.
“Protecting nature needs independent scientific oversight, not a mayoral team without the ecological skills who are under pressure to build new homes, schools, a theme park,” said Culver.
Crucially, transparency would disappear with the abolition of the quango.
“Loss of independent oversight also means loss of public knowledge,” said Culver. “Natural England can speak up when nature is in trouble. Governments have to explain why they ignored the regulator’s advice.”
Talk of the quango’s abolition smacks of a government not joining up its own dots. Until this week, government ministers were promoting a beefed up Natural England as the key to new planning reforms that would unlock growth.
The body was given the crucial role by ministers of managing and spending new levies that developers will be able to pay in order to sidestep environmental regulations and get spades in the ground more quickly.
The plan was for Natural England to use the hundreds of millions of pounds to create habitats to offset the damage caused by a particular development.
Environmental groups were assured by ministers that Natural England’s scientific expertise and legal duty to protect nature would ensure that the planning reforms were a “win, win” for nature and growth. On that assurance, many agreed to the changes.
But today that promise seems to lie in tatters, with ministers now suggesting the very same body is a block on development.
Environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole said: “Abolishing Natural England would give the Tories, Reform and their wealthy backers what they have always wanted – making it easier for landowners and developers to trash nature.
“Clement Attlee’s government created the forerunner to Natural England to protect our green and pleasant land. It would be a travesty for a Labour government to destroy it.”
